book_metadata.title: The Betrayal of Kast Pakistan
book_metadata.author: Lieutenant-General (R) A. A. K. Niazi HJ & BAR, SPK, SK, MC, PSC

claims.claim: East Pakistan Police, East Pakistan Rifles, Ansars, Fast Bengal Regiment battalions, and East Pakistani members of some regular units of the Army, Navy, and Air Force rebelled against the Government on 25 March 1971.
claims.actor: East Pakistan Police, East Pakistan Rifles, Ansars, Fast Bengal Regiment, and East Pakistani military personnel

claims.claim: The strength of Bengali armed forces that rebelled after 25 March 1971 was 162,000.
Approximately 125,000 civilians were trained by Russians and Indians in stages.
The total number of Bengalis in Mukti Bahini was 287,500.
50,000 personnel of the Indian Army joined Mukti Bahini in the garb of Muktis.
Thousands of armed Bengali dissidents helped the activities of Mukti Bahini.
The Awami League and other leftist organizations secretly organized underground militant wings and trained them in small-arms and terror tactics.
A separate force under the name of Mukti Bahini was formally created on 1 April 1971.
Colonel M. A. G. Osmany (Retd.) was appointed as the so-called C.-in-C of Mukti Bahini on 14 April 1971.
By May 1971, about fifty per cent of the insurgents had been disarmed.
The Indians set up fifty-nine camps along the border for training and equipping rebels.
claims.location: Border between East Pakistan and India

claims.claim: The Indians appointed a Major-General to organize and coordinate the training and indoctrination activities.
About 300 rebels were flown from Agartala to Cochin for underwater sabotage training.
About 300 frogmen were trained at Plassey on the Bhairathi River in West Bengal under Indian Navy and defected Pakistan Navy submariners.
claims.actor: Indian Navy and defected Pakistan Navy

claims.claim: The trainees were divided into three categories: Science Graduates, Undergraduates, and Non-matriculates, with different training regimens.
claims.event: Categorization of trainees for specialized training

claims.claim: An eight-member team of Russian experts was imparting guerrilla training to the rebels in India.
Special officer commissions were granted to selected students to establish a command structure within the rebels.
claims.event: Granting of officer commissions to rebels

claims.claim: About 600 young officers were trained at the Indian Military Academy, Dehra Dun.
claims.event: Training of young officers for rebels

claims.claim: The rebels were organized into regular units called SBR (Swadhin Bengal Regiments), each with a strength of 500.
The Indian Army raised two brigades of rebels at Tura, each with a strength of about 3,000 men.
A women’s wing of Mukti Bahini was established, but no special achievements were reported.
The entire area was divided into eight sectors, initially controlled by the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) and later taken over by the Indian Army.
claims.event: Division of East Pakistan into sectors

claims.claim: Brig. Shah Beg Singh and Brig. Jagjit Singh exercised overall command over the Bengali Brigades.
claims.actor: Brig. Shah Beg Singh, Brig. Jagjit Singh

claims.claim: The rebels organized two other forces: Poufan Bahini (Storm Troops) and Beman Bahini (Bangladesh Air Force).
The Indians were constructing an airfield for the rebels in Betai area with Russian financial and technical assistance.
By the end of June 1971, approximately 30,000 rebels had been trained in India.
By November 1971, about 70,000 rebels had been trained and 30,000 were undergoing training.
Limpet mines of Russian origin were captured from rebel frogmen by Pakistani troops.
Some American arms were recovered from the rebels, including a 57 mm RR captured at Chittagong.
Bangladeshi leaders approached Israel and possibly Japan for procurement of heavy weapons worth $2.5 million.
claims.event: Procurement of heavy weapons from foreign sources

claims.claim: Israel agreed to supply heavy weapons worth $2 million to Bangladesh within two months.
claims.event: Agreement to supply weapons to Bangladesh

claims.claim: The Indian Army provided wireless sets and other signals equipment to the rebels from their obsolete stock.
claims.event: Supply of communication equipment to rebels

claims.claim: The Indian Army supported the rebels in logistics and fire support, compensating for their weaknesses.
claims.event: Logistical and fire support to rebels

claims.claim: The local Bengali population provided intelligence, labor, and logistic facilities to the Indian Army.
The Indian Press exaggerated rebel successes in early stages but later downplayed Mukti Bahini’s role to glorify the Indian Army.
claims.event: Exaggeration and suppression of rebel achievements

claims.claim: The Indian Government denied the induction of regular troops as Mukti Bahini, but evidence like bridge explosions confirmed their involvement.
claims.event: Denial of troop involvement in Mukti Bahini

claims.claim: Morarji Desai confirmed that Mrs. Gandhi dispatched thousands of Indian soldiers disguised as Mukti Bahini, with 5,000 dying between April and December 1971.
claims.event: Disclosure about Indian troop involvement in Mukti Bahini

claims.claim: The East Pakistan Civil Armed Forces (EPCAF) had a strength of 13,000, mainly from West Pakistan and non-Bengali populations.
The Vulnerable Points Force (VPF) had a strength of 3,000 and was tasked with protecting critical infrastructure.
The Industrial Security Force (ISF) had a strength similar to the VPF and was tasked with protecting factories and industrial areas.
The EPCAF Special Force with a maximum strength of 10,000 was being raised but prevented from concentrating in East Pakistan due to hostilities.
The Old East Pakistan Police was demoralized and ineffective due to desertions and defections.
The New East Pakistan Police was formed to replace deserters and showed satisfactory performance against rebels.
The West Pakistan Police was brought to East Pakistan to reinforce local police forces.
Mujahid Battalions and Independent Mujahid Companies were employed on operational duties alongside regular forces.
claims.event: Employment on operational duties with regular forces

claims.claim: Mujahid Battalion Commanders started arriving in East Pakistan in November 1971.
The force was short of weapons and equipment.
claims.actor: Mujahid Battalions and Independent Mujahid Companies

claims.claim: A case was taken up with the Military Operations and Infantry Directorate at GHQ regarding weapon shortages.
claims.actor: Mujahid Battalions and Independent Mujahid Companies
claims.event: Request for weapons and equipment from GHQ

claims.claim: The proposal for raising an organized Razakar Force remained under consideration with HQ CMLA and GHQ for a long time.
Sanction for the raising of the Razakar Force was given at the end of August 1971.
Two separate wings, Al-Badr and Al-Shams, were organized within the Razakar Force.
claims.event: Organization of Al-Badr and Al-Shams wings

claims.claim: Well-educated students from schools and madrasas were trained in Al-Badr Wing for specialized operations.
claims.event: Training of students for specialized operations

claims.claim: Defection rates among Razakars were 4% in October 1971 and 6% in November 1971.
The Razakars were mostly employed in areas where army elements were present to control and utilize them.
The Razakars were harassed and intimidated by rebels, causing significant strain.
The Razakars required proper training but faced limitations due to the Eastern Command's operational commitments.
claims.event: Limitation in providing training to Razakars

claims.claim: 70% of the target ceiling of 50,000 Razakars was achieved across all districts.
Battle schools were established to train Razakar platoon and company commanders.
claims.event: Establishment of battle schools for training

claims.claim: About sixty young officers were selected as Razakar Group Commanders.
The Razakars were equipped with only 275 light machine-guns and 390 sten guns, far below the required 2,500 each.
The Razakars felt they were not trusted with superior arms, exacerbating their morale and performance issues.
claims.event: Perceived lack of trust in weapon allocation

claims.claim: The Razakars were mixed with West Pakistani police and non-Bengali elements to maintain control.
claims.event: Integration with West Pakistani police and non-Bengalis

claims.claim: The mission given to the Commander, Eastern Command, was to evict guerrillas and prevent territory from falling into enemy hands.
Lieutenant-General Tikka Khan was Martial Law Administrator and operated independently from the Commander, Eastern Command.
claims.event: Role as Martial Law Administrator with operational independence

claims.claim: The Government was confined to the President's House, with Generals Yahya, Hamid, Peerzada, Omar, and Mitha managing state affairs.
claims.event: Confinement to President's House during crisis

claims.claim: Lieutenant-General Gul Hassan, Chief of General Staff, did not issue operational instructions for counter-insurgency or East Pakistan defense.
The Indian Army was training Mukti Bahini in India with Russian guerrilla experts.
claims.event: Training of Mukti Bahini with Russian advisors

claims.claim: No artillery or tanks were sent to the Eastern Command despite repeated requests.
claims.event: Refusal to provide heavy weapons and tanks

claims.claim: Soldiers had to fight barefoot and bare-chested due to lack of ordnance stores.
claims.event: Lack of basic equipment leading to poor combat conditions

claims.claim: General Hamid reaffirmed the political mission of not allowing any territory to fall to rebels in September 1971.
Indian forces were reported to be building roads along the eastern border from Karianganj to Chittagong by October 1971.
The enemy threat included three divisions plus a Mukti Bahini brigade targeting Sylhet, Bhairab Bazar, and Chandpur.
claims.event: Reported offensive plans against East Pakistan

claims.claim: Ad hoc formations were created for deception and defensive positioning against anticipated enemy threats.
claims.event: Creation of ad hoc units for strategic purposes

claims.claim: Border outposts (BOPs) were manned by Mujahids, Razakars, Scouts, and Rangers to protect lines of communication.
claims.event: Deployment at border outposts for defense

claims.claim: Regular troops were concentrated in strong points and fortresses to fight defensive battles.
claims.event: Concentration of troops for defensive operations

claims.claim: The concept of defense involved multiple layers to impose attrition on the enemy and delay their advance.
Fortresses were designated as no-penetration lines where troops would fight to the death.
claims.event: Designation of fortresses for last-ditch defense

claims.claim: The fate of East Pakistan and the entire country depended on the Western Garrison's success in West Pakistan.
Units were augmented with Mujahids and CAF to strengthen defensive capabilities.
claims.event: Integration of Mujahids and CAF into regular units

claims.claim: Punjis (sharpened bamboo sticks) were used to hamper enemy movement and channelize attacks.
claims.event: Deployment of punjis for defensive purposes

claims.claim: Reorganization of divisions and brigades was completed by the end of October 1971.
The ad hoc 202 Brigade was created in Sylhet under Brigadier Salimullah.
The ad hoc 314 Brigade was created for the Khulna sector under Colonel Fazal Hamid.
The ad hoc 91 Independent Brigade was created in Chittagong under Brigadier Ata Malik.
claims.event: Formation of ad hoc 91 Independent Brigade

claims.claim: The ad hoc 36 Division was created at Dhaka under Major-General Jamshed.
The ad hoc 39 Division was raised under Major-General M. Rahim Khan to defend Chandpur.
GHQ did not send the promised replacement forces for Dhaka.
Field artillery was proportionally distributed due to shortages, not allocated one regiment per brigade.
claims.event: Artillery allocation strategy due to scarcity

claims.claim: Ad hoc formations lacked trained staff, officers, and transport but used existing communication resources.
claims.event: Resource limitations in ad hoc formations

claims.claim: The operational plan emphasized forward defensive posture and trading space for time to inflict attrition on the enemy.
The East Pakistan Civil Armed Forces had disintegrated, leading to reliance on local Razakars for border defense.
Local Razakars, mainly ex-Biharis and loyal East Pakistanis, were trained to man border outposts.
claims.event: Training of local recruits for border defense

claims.claim: The East Pakistani government recommended sealing borders as a top priority due to Indian support for rebels.
Dhaka was identified as the linchpin of the defense strategy, with fortresses and strong points acting as barriers.
claims.event: Designation of Dhaka as strategic center

claims.claim: GHQ and ISI Directorate failed to inform the Eastern Command about heliborne threats or Indian military capabilities.
The plan was discussed and finalized in a formation commanders’ conference attended by General Jamshed.
COAS General Hamid visited the Eastern Command in October 1971 and was briefed on changes to the defense plan.
The plan was functional under prevailing circumstances, despite political constraints and resource shortages.
The High Command did not interfere with how the commander used tools to achieve missions, as long as tasks were clear.
claims.event: Policy of non-interference in operational execution

claims.claim: The High Command intentionally put the Eastern Command at the mercy of the Indian Army by giving them the initiative.
claims.event: Strategic decision to allow Indian initiative

claims.claim: The Eastern Command had to guess and remain alert for contingencies due to lack of clear enemy intentions.
The Indian Army was reported to be constructing roads along the eastern border from Karianganj to Chittagong, expected to be ready by October 1971.
The Indian Army was reported to have nineteen engineer battalions and significant bridging equipment deployed.
claims.event: Deployment of engineering units and equipment

claims.claim: The Eastern Command's plan was revised to include ad hoc formations for deception and defensive positioning.
claims.event: Revised operational plan with ad hoc units

claims.claim: The Eastern Command's defense concept relied on fortresses and strong points to restrict enemy maneuverability.
The East Pakistan Civil Armed Forces had disintegrated, leading to reliance on local Razakars for border defense.
The Eastern Command received intelligence that India was unlikely to launch an all-out war but might conduct nibbling attacks.
The Eastern Command recommended sealing borders as a top priority due to Indian support for rebels.
The Eastern Command's defense plan was based on rivers and water obstacles as natural barriers.
claims.event: Use of geographical features for defense

claims.claim: The Eastern Command's plan was discussed and finalized in a formation commanders’ conference attended by General Jamshed.
The Eastern Command's plan was incorporated into the 'Order of Battle' issued by GHQ in October 1971.
claims.event: Incorporation of defense plan into official order

claims.claim: The Pakistani military used deception strategies to mislead the enemy about troop strength.
claims.event: Implementation of a deception plan involving flags, maps, and local Bengali cooperation.

claims.claim: Major-General Jamshed was mistaken for the Divisional Commander of the Fourth Division during troop visits.
claims.event: Being mistaken for a higher-ranking officer to deceive Indian forces.

claims.claim: The Pakistani military used four miniature flags and maps in their office to simulate the presence of four divisions.
claims.event: Deployment of visual deception tactics (flags, maps) to mislead Indian intelligence.

claims.claim: Indian Army commanders admitted that they believed the Pakistani Eastern Garrison had four divisions.
claims.event: Admission of misjudging Pakistani troop strength based on deception.
claims.source: Major-General Sukhwant Singh (book: The Liberation of Bangladesh)

claims.claim: The Indian Army's advance was cautious due to the belief that the 36 ad hoc Division was a full-fledged division.
claims.event: Delayed advance along northern routes due to misperceptions about Pakistani troop strength.

claims.claim: Brigadier Shah Beg (later Major-General) questioned the number of divisions in East Pakistan after surrender.
claims.event: Post-surrender inquiry about Pakistani troop strength and command structure.

claims.claim: Brigadier Kler (later Major-General) questioned why the Indian Army did not rush to capture Dhaka despite advantages.
claims.event: Post-surrender analysis of Indian military strategy and challenges in East Pakistan.

claims.claim: Lieutenant-General Sagat Singh acknowledged that Dhaka was well-defended with multiple divisions and reinforcements.
claims.event: Admission of the difficulty in capturing Dhaka due to Pakistani defenses.

claims.claim: The Indian Army faced challenges in outflanking Dhaka due to the presence of the Bhairab Brigade.
claims.event: Strategic difficulties in attacking Dhaka due to Pakistani troop positioning.

claims.claim: General Sagat Singh requested seven days for preparation and assembly of troops before attacking Dhaka.
claims.event: Request for time to prepare due to logistical challenges.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's failure to capture Dhaka despite overwhelming resources was attributed to Pakistani deception and strong defenses.
claims.event: Failure to achieve military objectives in East Pakistan due to misjudged troop strength and effective Pakistani resistance.

claims.claim: General Arora was retired immediately after the war and not given any other job.
claims.event: Post-war retirement due to failure in East Pakistan campaign.

claims.claim: Maulana Mufti Mahmood advised against using force and advocated for a political solution to the East Pakistan crisis.
claims.event: Advocacy for political resolution over military action.

claims.claim: The Pakistani government appointed a civilian Governor and ministers as part of efforts toward political settlement.
claims.event: Appointment of civilian leadership in East Pakistan.

claims.claim: By-elections were announced, leading to increased political activity among rightists and loyal Bengalis.
claims.event: Announcement of by-elections to restore political processes.

claims.claim: The Pakistani military recommended amnesty for rebels, but implementation was delayed and partial.
claims.event: Delayed and incomplete amnesty program for rebels.

claims.claim: The Pakistani intelligence network collapsed due to defections in favor of the Awami League.
claims.event: Disintegration of intelligence networks during military action.

claims.claim: The Indian Army was under the impression that Dhaka was defended by an entire division, including the 36 ad hoc Division.
claims.event: Misjudgment of Pakistani troop strength in Dhaka sector.

claims.claim: The Indian Army faced heavy casualties and logistical challenges despite overwhelming resources.
claims.event: High casualty rates and logistical difficulties in East Pakistan campaign.

claims.claim: The Pakistani military had approximately 30,000 troops deployed in Dhaka, including retired personnel and civilians.
claims.event: Deployment of a large force in Dhaka, including non-combatants.

claims.claim: The Indian Army was unable to capture Dhaka despite having air superiority and naval support.
claims.event: Failure to capitalize on strategic advantages in East Pakistan.

claims.claim: The Pakistani military had Russian experts training guerrillas and handling sophisticated weapons during the conflict.
claims.event: Involvement of Russian experts in training and logistics.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's failure to capture Dhaka was attributed to the effectiveness of Pakistani deception tactics.
claims.event: Acknowledgment of the success of Pakistani deception strategies.

claims.claim: The Pakistani military had three Major-Generals, one Air Commodore, and multiple Brigadiers in Dhaka.
claims.event: High-ranking officers stationed in Dhaka during the conflict.

claims.claim: The Indian Army was forced to shift landing areas due to the presence of the Bhairab Brigade.
claims.event: Adjustment of military operations due to Pakistani troop movements.

claims.claim: The Indian Army could not bring tanks and artillery into East Pakistan due to the Bhairab Brigade's presence.
claims.event: Logistical challenges in deploying heavy equipment.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's advance was hindered by the lack of medium and heavy artillery for shelling Dhaka.
claims.event: Inability to conduct effective artillery bombardment due to shortages.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's failure to capture Dhaka was attributed to the Pakistani military's use of deception and strong defenses.
claims.event: Acknowledgment of the effectiveness of Pakistani strategies.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's invasion plan was based on the assumption that four divisions were deployed in East Pakistan.
claims.event: Miscalculation of Pakistani troop strength leading to strategic delays.

claims.claim: The Indian Army did not rush to capture Faridpur after suffering losses in Kushtia due to misjudged troop strength.
claims.event: Strategic hesitation based on incorrect assumptions about Pakistani forces.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's failure to achieve military objectives in East Pakistan was attributed to political decisions by Yahya and Bhutto.
claims.event: Acknowledgment of political factors influencing the conflict outcome.

claims.claim: The Pakistani military had enough weapons to arm thousands of people, including retired personnel and civilians.
claims.event: Arming of non-combatants as part of defense strategy.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's failure to capture Dhaka was attributed to the Pakistani military's use of deception and strong defenses.
claims.event: Acknowledgment of the effectiveness of Pakistani strategies.

claims.claim: The Indian Army's failure to capture Dhaka was attributed to the Pakistani military's use of deception and strong defenses.
claims.event: Acknowledgment of the effectiveness of Pakistani strategies.

claims.claim: Neither ISI nor MI Directorates warned us of the Indian helicopter-gunship capability encountered during the war.
claims.event: Failure to warn about Indian helicopter-gunship capability

claims.claim: Pakistan had to resort to deception, bluff, and whispering campaigns due to lack of intelligence resources.
Bhutto visited China in early November 1971 and met Zhou Enlai on 7 November.
claims.event: Visit to China and meeting with Zhou Enlai

claims.claim: The Chinese Acting Foreign Minister accused India of interfering in Pakistan’s internal affairs.
Indian planners considered the possibility of collusion between Pakistan and China.
A conspiracy to carry out a coup against Yahya involved Lt.-Gen. Gul Hassan and Air Marshal Rahim Khan.
claims.actor: Lt.-Gen. Gul Hassan, Air Marshal Rahim Khan
claims.event: Planning of a coup against Yahya

claims.claim: General Hamid advised against starting a war in the west due to potential Chinese threats.
Pakistan attacked India on 3 December 1971 without informing East Pakistan.
The Indian Air Force crippled Pakistani mobility and air support.
claims.event: Disruption of Pakistani mobility and air support

claims.claim: The Indian Navy imposed a sea blockade, isolating East Pakistan from West Pakistan.
The Russians openly joined the war on the Indian side.
claims.event: Support for India in the war

claims.claim: General Hamid refused to use the 'hump route' for communication during the blockade.
The attack on the West was part of a plan to isolate and defeat East Pakistan.
claims.event: Strategic planning to isolate East Pakistan

claims.claim: Major-General Fazal Muqeem described the state of troops in East Pakistan.
The 14 Infantry Division faced stress from Martial Law duties and counter-insurgency operations.
Pakistani troops lacked proper equipment and training for counter-insurgency operations.
claims.event: Lack of anti-guerrilla training and resources

claims.claim: The enemy (Mukti Bahini) did not follow conventional warfare rules.
Pakistani troops fought for eight months against Indian and rebel activities.
Indian artillery and mortar fire intensified since September 1971.
Pakistani troops were deployed in platoons and sections across wide areas.
Pakistani troops faced no relief, leading to exhaustion and lack of rest.
Enemy agents infiltrated civil government and local populations, causing security issues.
Casualties from guerrilla activities added to troop strain.
The public in West Pakistan did not appreciate the challenges faced by East Pakistani forces.
claims.event: Lack of awareness about East Pakistan’s struggles

claims.claim: Foreign experts estimated 250,000–300,000 trained troops were needed for counter-insurgency in East Pakistan.
Pakistan had only three infantry divisions without heavy weapons.
claims.event: Limited military resources in East Pakistan

claims.claim: India supported Mukti Bahini with men, material, and technical training.
Pakistani government failed to provide political and psychological support for troops.
claims.event: Lack of political backing for East Pakistani forces

claims.claim: West Pakistan was not united behind Eastern troops.
claims.event: Lack of solidarity with East Pakistani forces

claims.claim: Pakistani troops succeeded in initial objectives despite overwhelming odds.
India’s pressure on borders affected troop morale and fear of isolation.
The President did not visit East Pakistan during critical months.
Indian propaganda exploited the President’s absence to undermine Pakistani morale.
Pakistani troops felt isolated and homesick due to lack of leadership presence.
Speculation arose about the President’s absence from East Pakistan.
claims.event: Rumors and speculation about President’s intentions

claims.claim: Pakistani troops desired direct leadership presence for morale.
claims.event: Desire to see C-in-C in person

claims.claim: The President did not visit East Pakistan since March 1971.
Pakistani Army’s performance was described as a miracle despite challenges.
India’s pressure on borders affected troop morale and fear of isolation.
The President’s absence led to troops feeling abandoned.
claims.event: Perceived abandonment of East Pakistani forces

claims.claim: Pakistani troops were engaged in undefined operations without clear objectives.
Pakistani troops maintained confidence despite hardships.
Pakistani forces lacked heavy weapons and logistic support in East Pakistan.
claims.event: Limited military resources in East Pakistan

claims.claim: PAF squadron strength was reduced due to frequent use.
Pakistani Navy’s gunboats were insufficient for controlling rivers and sea routes.
claims.event: Limited naval capabilities in East Pakistan

claims.claim: India’s massive invasion was anticipated as a strategic threat.
claims.event: Imminent large-scale invasion of East Pakistan

claims.claim: Support from West Pakistan was needed to maintain morale in East Pakistan.
claims.event: Need for logistical and moral support

claims.claim: General Hamid refused additional troops and resources for Eastern Command.
Pakistani military strategy emphasized West Pakistan’s role in defending East Pakistan.
General Niazi briefed GHQ on enemy actions and troop deployment.
India was expected to launch an attack when terrain in East Pakistan was dry and Chinese passes were blocked.
Mukti Bahini and guerrilla activities increased significantly.
Indian troop concentrations along borders were reported.
War was anticipated as enemy build-up completed in November/December.
Operational environment was not conducive to full-fledged war.
Guerrilla activities targeted infrastructure and local populations.
claims.event: Sabotage of bridges, roads, and railways

claims.claim: Civil administration in East Pakistan was symbolic with Razakars and Mujahids maintaining control.
Industrial workers restored production to 80% under threat.
Major cities in East Pakistan functioned normally despite guerrilla attacks.
Recommendation for amnesty and political solution to simplify dealing with invaders.
India’s military strength was estimated as 11–12 divisions plus other units.
Russo-Indian Pact of 1971 strengthened India’s strategic position.
Indian Mountain Divisions were concentrated forward for encirclement.
Army and command engineer resources were allocated to Corps.
Tracks and roads were improved in Tripura area.
Aggressive activities along borders were intensified.
Indian Prime Minister visited abroad to garner sympathy and support.
Hypotheses about rebel activities and Indian involvement were submitted.
H-1: Intensification of rebel activity leading to territory capture and Bangladesh establishment.
H-2: Full-scale Indian offensive with H-1 in progress.
H-3: If no results from H-1, proceed to H-2.
GHQ was warned that the best time for an offensive by Pakistan would be before October or May.
Three courses were proposed for prosecuting the war against India.
Pulling back troops could lead to loss of territory and disintegration of Pakistan.
Holding borders strongly risked defeat in detail and unnecessary casualties.
Attrition warfare could benefit rebels and Indians while allowing raids into India.
GHQ agreed with the third course of action to fight an undeclared war against the Indian Army and deal with rebels in East Pakistan.
A Central Psychological Warfare Board was recommended to be established in Dhaka to indoctrinate the population.
Normalcy was recommended to be restored as soon as possible to maintain public morale.
Agartala airfield was to be engaged to retaliate against Indian firing.
Civil administration was to be strengthened with support for law and order agencies and paramilitary forces like Razakars.
Additional troops were inducted into East Pakistan to fight an undeclared war against the Indian Army and rebels.
No war should be started in West Pakistan.
claims.event: Recommendation against starting war in West Pakistan

claims.claim: COAS General Abdul Hamid Khan insisted on maintaining a forward defensive posture and fighting insurgents.
claims.actor: General Abdul Hamid Khan (Chief of Army Staff)
claims.event: Insistence on defensive posture and counter-insurgency
claims.source: Major-General Jamshed and Brig. Baqir Siddiqui

claims.claim: GHQ partially agreed to requests for additional artillery and troops, promising eight infantry battalions and one engineer battalion.
claims.source: Major-General Jamshed and Brig. Baqir Siddiqui

claims.claim: India was expected to attack East Pakistan on Eid Day (21 November 1971).
claims.source: Major-General Jamshed and Brig. Baqir Siddiqui

claims.claim: The CGS (Chief of General Staff) was involved in a coup d’état to transfer power to Bhutto.
The C.-in-C. Navy suggested switching forces to East Pakistan if no war was started in West Pakistan.
39 ad hoc Division was raised under Major-General M. Rahim Khan with staff from HQ Martial Law.
53 Brigade was moved to Chodagram-Laxam despite being the Command Reserve for Dhaka’s defense.
The relative strength of opposing forces in Sylhet-Chittagong Sector was outlined with specific troop numbers.
India deployed 4 Corps with 8, 23, and 57 Divisions in the Sylhet-Chittagong Sector.
Pakistan’s 14 and 39 Divisions had eleven battalions in the Sylhet-Chittagong Sector.
The ratio of troops between Pakistan and India was approximately one to ten.
The hostile population in East Pakistan provided support to the Indian Army.
The Indian Army invaded East Pakistan with the strength of twelve divisions.
The total strength of Indian forces for Bangladesh liberation exceeded a third of a million.
The Indian Army had 17 squadrons of LAF, SU-7, and MIG-21 aircraft.
The Indian Navy had a carrier squadron including Vikrant.
The Indian Army had a ratio of one to four in East Pakistan (excluding air and naval contingents).
American intelligence estimated the troop ratio in East Pakistan as one to six.
The Indian Army had superior numbers, equipment, and strategic positioning.
The Indian Army could not defeat the Pakistan Eastern Garrison despite overwhelming superiority.
The situation on the eve of Eid Day (21 November 1971) involved concentrated Pakistani troops and Indian attacks in multiple salients.
Razakars and Mujahids replaced counter-insurgency troops in East Pakistan.
Pakistani troops were fatigued due to prolonged operations in hostile conditions.
Pakistani divisions lacked tank regiments, medium guns, and artillery.
The second-line forces were not fully equipped or trained.
GHQ asked about the progress of clearing salients occupied by Mukti Bahini.
Only two battalions instead of eight were received from GHQ.
The enemy was poised for a major offensive on 21 November 1971.
An ad hoc Division was created at Chandpur to execute the operational plan.
Defensive positions in East Pakistan lacked concrete structures and artillery cover.
No funds were allocated for defense works in East Pakistan.
claims.event: Lack of funding for military infrastructure

claims.claim: Mines were used against Mukti Bahini but were ineffective against the Indian Army.
Artillery was insufficient to counter Indian attacks in East Pakistan.
Obsolescent M-24 light tanks were sent to East Pakistan.
Anti-tank guns and heavy artillery were insufficient to counter Indian armor.
No air support was available for Pakistani forces in East Pakistan.
The local population provided detailed intelligence to the Indian Army.
claims.event: Support for Indian forces through intelligence sharing

claims.claim: Pakistani troops had been fighting continuously for eight months without relief.
Senior army doctors reported troops had reached battle exhaustion in August 1971.
claims.actor: Army medical team from West Pakistan
claims.event: Report on troop health and exhaustion

claims.claim: A campaign to instill the spirit of jihad was initiated to raise troop morale.
The motto 'With the board or on the board' was adopted by Pakistani troops.
The geography of East Pakistan defied centralized control and mutual support between divisions.
claims.event: Challenges in military coordination due to terrain

claims.claim: Troops faced disorientation and ambushes due to hostile fire in East Pakistan.
claims.event: Operational challenges from terrain and insurgency

claims.claim: By November 1971, troops had lived in waterlogged bunkers with slime and vermin.
Pakistani troops were inadequately clothed and shod, leading to physical ailments.
Pakistani troops lost less territory in East Pakistan compared to West Pakistan during the war.
claims.event: Comparison of territorial losses between sectors

claims.claim: Pakistani troops in East Pakistan were subjected to captivity and questioning after surrender.
Indian troops had the advantage of fresh supplies and bases in West Bengal, Assam, and Tripura.
The Bengalis supported the Indian Army in their 'War of Liberation'.
The Indians had increased border raids and artillery fire.
claims.event: Increased border raids and artillery fire

claims.claim: Pakistan had been completely isolated diplomatically, politically, militarily, and psychologically due to the faulty foreign policy of Yahya’s Government.
claims.event: Diplomatic, political, military, and psychological isolation

claims.claim: Indian propaganda was so well organized and effective that it won universal sympathy for the Bangladesh cause.
claims.event: Propaganda efforts to gain international sympathy for Bangladesh

claims.claim: The Indian Army chose the invasion date based on monsoon conditions and China’s intervention options.
claims.event: Strategic timing of invasion considering monsoons and Chinese threat
